ideas.name: Click-RAM: a snap-through 2D-nanoribbon mechanical floating gate over an oxide channel
ideas.one_liner: Store the bit as which way a pre-buckled 50-100 nm graphene, MoS2 or ALD ribbon is bent; the ribbon is the suspended gate of an oxide read transistor, so there is no stored charge to leak, nothing to refresh and nothing for row hammer to disturb.
ideas.mechanism: A ribbon of graphene, monolayer MoS2 or ~2 nm ALD Al2O3/TiN, 50-100 nm long and 10-20 nm wide, is clamped at both ends over a sealed 3.5-6 nm cavity with 0.1-0.3% built-in compressive strain, so it has two stable buckled shapes (+q and -q, q = 1.2-2.3 nm) that never touch the floor. An IGZO (or Si) channel under the cavity is the bottom electrode: a 1.9-2.8 V pulse between ribbon and channel snaps the ribbon down; a pulse on a top plate snaps it up. Read: hold the ribbon at ~0.8 V as a suspended gate; the up/down gap changes gate coupling ~1.5x, which gives a ~10^3 channel-current ratio while the read force is only 18% of the snap force (non-destructive). Cells sit in BEOL tiers above CMOS periphery. Because the state is mechanical, retention is set by a ~45-80 kT elastic barrier, not by leakage.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 access-device leakage tail and refresh (removed: retention is mechanical); A1 #1 capacitor wall (no capacitor); A1 #8 destructive read (read is non-destructive); A1 #9 row hammer (no stored charge to disturb); A2 white space 2 (use-phase energy).
ideas.step_change_claim: Refresh energy and standby power go to zero (non-volatile); intrinsic write energy is ~2-4 aJ, versus ~3 fJ stored on a 1-beta cell plus ~46 fJ per refresh; mechanical switching is sub-ns (f0 = 2-15 GHz). Density reaches 1-beta parity only with two BEOL tiers of 50 nm ribbons. The step change is on energy and volatility, not density.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Clamped buckled ribbon, first mode: barrier dU = E*A*pi^4*q^4/(32*L^3) (derived in the model). L=100 nm, w=20 nm graphene (E2D 340 N/m), 80 kT barrier: q = +/-2.0 nm, 0.10% strain, k_eff 0.66 N/m, f0 5.4 GHz, snap force 0.26 nN at 1.92 V across an 8 nm gap, electrode C*V^2 = 4.1 aJ. L=50, w=10 nm: q = +/-1.41 nm, f0 15 GHz, 2.8 V, 3.5 aJ (45 kT version: 2.2 V, 2.2 aJ); MoS2: f0 2.3-6.5 GHz. B5-00: a 16Gb die needs ~44 kT for 1 s and ~64 kT for 10 years, so 80 kT is non-volatile. Pull-in: at the down state the electrostatic negative stiffness is 0.51 vs 0.66 N/m (L=100: marginal) but 1.9 vs 1.3 N/m (L=50: pulls in), so short ribbons need charge-controlled or pulse-terminated drive. Read: coupling ratio 1.47 gives a 0.26 V effective-drive difference at 0.8 V, ~10^3.4 at 75 mV/dec. Area: 5,600 nm2 (L=100) = 5.2x a 1-beta cell; 2,250 nm2 (L=50, 25 nm pitch) = 2.1x; two tiers = 1.05x. Fatigue reference: a 5 MHz MEMS oscillator runs 1.6e15 cycles in 10 years. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-01)

ideas.novelty: NEW combination. Buckled-beam NEMS memories (Tsuchiya/Mizuta/Oda; Charlot) and suspended-gate FETs are KNOWN. The new part is a non-contact 2D or ALD ribbon sized for a 45-80 kT barrier, used as the suspended gate of an oxide read transistor in stacked BEOL tiers as a DRAM replacement. B1-18 (a NEMS relay as an access switch) is a different cell.
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) Pull-in and stiction: one touch and van der Waals adhesion (~0.3-0.45 J/m2 x 2e-15 m2 = ~1e-15 J, more than 1,000x the barrier) welds the ribbon permanently. (2) Strain uniformity: the barrier goes as q^4, so a +/-10% strain spread gives roughly +/-20% barrier and snap-voltage spread across 1e10 ribbons. (3) Release, vacuum sealing and contamination of suspended ribbons at 25-40 nm pitch; gas damping and moisture in nm gaps.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Charge-controlled (current-pulse) actuation, which is stable over the full gap in MEMS; low-adhesion stoppers (hBN, or a fluorine-free monolayer coating); keep q at or below 0.4 of the gap. (2) Tune stress through ALD thickness and anneal, or measure and trim: write-verify picks per-row snap voltages and ECC absorbs the tail. (3) MEMS wafer-level vacuum sealing with sacrificial carbon or a-Si released by O2 plasma or XeF2 (no HF), first on 200 mm BEOL.
ideas.million_dollar_demo: Months 0-9: FEM and TCAD of ribbon plus IGZO channel; three lengths x three strains (~$50k with tools). Months 6-18: university nanofab run of 1 kb arrays of suspended MoS2/graphene or ALD ribbons over IGZO channels, using wafer-scale 2D films (~$250k for fab and materials). Months 12-24: measure snap thresholds, 1e12-cycle endurance on a pulse tester, ns switching with RF pulses, and thermally activated flip rates at 150-250 C to extract the barrier (~$100k test). Success means at least 45 kT inferred, 1e12 cycles without drift, at most 3 V, and sub-10 ns. Total ~$400k of non-salary spend.
ideas.resource_angle: Ribbons are C, Mo/S or Al/O: no Hf, no Ru, no capacitor high-aspect-ratio etch (fewer PFAS etch steps), and almost no use-phase refresh energy. The IGZO channel carries A2's gallium flag; In-Sn-Zn-O avoids Ga.

ideas.name: Capacitor-hole racetrack: electroplated domain-wall nanowires in DRAM's high-aspect-ratio mold
ideas.one_liner: Keep the 1.3-3 um deep capacitor holes DRAM fabs already etch, fill them bottom-up with electroplated CoNi or NiFe, and shift 10-25 magnetic domains per hole past a top read head. That is ~10x the bits per cell footprint, with no capacitor and no refresh.
ideas.mechanism: Etch the standard honeycomb hole lattice (~20 nm diameter at 35-40 nm pitch) in oxide. Instead of conformal ALD electrodes, electroplate a magnetic nanowire up from a seed at the hole bottom, modulating composition (Co-rich/Ni-rich, or thin Cu spacers) every ~60 nm to make pinning notches. Bits are axial domains separated by Bloch-point domain walls, which cylindrical wires carry without the Walker breakdown that slows flat racetracks. A vertical select transistor under each hole (4F2/6F2 vertical-channel style) drives ~30 uA bipolar shift pulses through the wire. A 20 nm MTJ on the planarised top reads the top bit and writes it (STT, or SOT from a top heavy-metal line). Half of each track is shift buffer, giving 10 data bits per 1.3 um hole and 25 per 3 um hole.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 capacitor wall (no capacitor); A1 #2 no manufacturable 3D cell (bits stacked along z with one etch and one plating step); A1 #3 refresh (non-volatile); A1 #4 litho-bound scaling (density comes from hole height, not F); A1 #9 row hammer (no charge).
ideas.step_change_claim: ~10x (1.3 um holes) to ~25x (3 um holes) bits per 1-beta cell footprint: 4.5-11 Gb/mm2 in principle, or 1-beta density at ~3x larger F with no EUV. Refresh energy goes to zero.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Bit length ~3 wire diameters = 60 nm, so a 1,300 nm hole has 21.7 slots and 10 data bits (half buffer); a 3,000 nm hole has 25. Shift: J = 1e11 A/m2 in a 20 nm wire is 31 uA (inside a vertical access transistor's on-current); R = rho*L/A = 828 ohm at 2e-7 ohm.m; 0.82 uW. At ~100 m/s, a third of the ~300 m/s simulated for current-driven Bloch-point walls, one bit-shift takes 0.6 ns and an average 5-shift access 3 ns, costing 2.5 fJ. At 1e12 A/m2 the shift needs 314 uA and 82 fJ, too much for a cell transistor. Read: a 20 nm MTJ at RA 5 ohm.um2 is 16 kohm, and 10 uA gives ~80 mV at 100% TMR. Material: 2.9e13 holes per wafer hold 0.1 g of magnetic metal, 2.3 t/yr for the whole DRAM fleet. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-02)

Racetrack memory (Parkin, IBM, whose original proposal used vertical tracks), Bloch-point wall dynamics in cylindrical wires (Fernandez-Roldan, Chubykalo-Fesenko, Tejo, Bran and co-workers) and electroplating magnetic nanowires in AAO templates are all KNOWN. ideas.show_stoppers: (1) Shift current density of 1e11-1e12 A/m2, against ~1e10 A/m2 DC electromigration rules for Cu, plus Joule heating in a dense array. (2) Uniform pinning: plated grain structure, diameter fluctuation and notch variation make domains skip or stick, and a single shift error corrupts a serial track. (3) A read/write head on top of every wire at 35-40 nm pitch, which is MRAM's hardest patterning problem.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Ferrimagnetic or compensated alloys and spin-orbit-assisted motion to cut threshold J by ~10x; bipolar, low-duty pulses, since electromigration life improves under AC. (2) Guard domains, parity and read-after-shift verification, as racetrack proposals do; pulse-reverse plating for uniform nanocrystalline wires. (3) Share one MTJ among 2-4 wires through a lateral SOT collector line, or read by anomalous Hall in a crossbar of top lines.
ideas.million_dollar_demo: Plate CoNi and NiFe wires into commercial AAO and into university-etched SiO2 hole arrays (20-40 nm, 1-3 um deep) at a university electrochemistry lab (~$80k). Image domain-wall motion with MFM and XMCD at a national-lab light source, and measure single-wire magnetoresistance with e-beam-defined contacts (~$150k). Then build a 16-wire test chip with top MTJs on a university magnetics line (~$250k). Success means deterministic 10-bit shifting at or below 1e11 A/m2 and a shift-error rate below 1e-6 over 1e10 shifts.
ideas.resource_angle: No capacitor dielectric (Hf/Zr) and no Ru electrodes. Co is concentrated in the DRC, but fleet-wide use is only ~2.3 t/yr, and NiFe permalloy avoids Co. Electroplating is low-temperature, low-energy and PFAS-free. Density from height cuts EUV dependence.

ideas.name: Deep-level charge bit: QD-Flash physics shrunk toward an atom-placed single-defect cell
ideas.one_liner: Store one to a few charges in a deliberately placed ~1.0-1.3 eV deep state under a 10-15 nm gate. Capture writes in ns, thermal emission is too slow to matter for seconds to days, and each charge shifts the read transistor by 20-46 mV.
ideas.mechanism: Ensemble version (exists): self-assembled GaSb or InGaSb quantum dots in a GaP matrix give ~1 eV hole localisation. A gate bias floods the dots with holes (capture, ns), and a reverse field empties them by field-assisted emission (350 ns measured, ~10 ns predicted). The stored charge sits above a channel whose conductance is read non-destructively. Single-defect version (2040 tools): hydrogen-depassivation lithography or deterministic single-ion implantation places 1-3 deep-level dopants or engineered defects in a crystalline barrier under a 10-15 nm gate. Each trapped charge is a quantised threshold step, so the cell is natively multi-level (bits = number of charges). No amorphous tunnel oxide sits in the write path, so there is no oxide wear.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 capacitor wall (1-3 electrons stored instead of ~17,700); A1 #3 refresh (retention set by choosing the level depth); A1 #4 litho (~4F2 at F = 10-14 nm with 2 bits/cell).
ideas.step_change_claim: [SPECULATIVE] 2.7-5x density (4F2 at F = 10 nm, 1-2 bits/cell), ~3.5 aJ gate write energy, and a refresh interval anywhere from 1 s to 1 day by picking a 1.0-1.3 eV level.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Emission time tau = exp(E/kT)/(sigma*v*N) with sigma 1e-15 cm2, v 1e7 cm/s, N 1e19 cm-3 (prefactor 1e-11 s). For 1 s at a raw BER of 1e-6: E >= 39 kT = 1.01 eV at 300 K, 1.21 eV at 85 C. For at most one flip per 1.7e10 bits in 1 s: 1.26 / 1.51 eV. For 1 day at a raw BER of 1e-6: 1.31 / 1.56 eV. QD-Flash's 4-day record implies ~0.98 eV with this prefactor. Capture at n = 1e18 cm-3 takes 0.1 ns (6 ns measured). One electron under a 10 / 15 / 20 nm gate at EOT 1 nm shifts Vt by 46 / 21 / 12 mV. Poole-Frenkel lowering at 1 MV/cm is only 0.23 eV (x7,000 in rate), so erase must use band-to-trap tunnelling at high field, not barrier lowering alone. 4F2 at F = 10 nm is 400 nm2/bit (2.7x 1-beta density); 2 bits/cell gives 5.3x. Gate C*V^2 at 10 nm and 1 V is 3.5 aJ. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-03)

ideas.name: Jot-RAM: image-sensor pinned wells and correlated double sampling for few-electron multi-level memory
ideas.one_liner: Image sensors already read 0.22 electrons rms at room temperature, with 0.1 electron/s of dark current. Build a 'pixel without light' (a vertical pinned storage well, a transfer gate and a shared floating diffusion) and store 4 bits as 0-320 electrons.
ideas.mechanism: Each cell is a vertical buried n-well in p-Si, ~40 nm wide and ~600 nm deep, holding ~450 electrons. A p+ sheath pins the well so surface and sidewall states stay filled and cannot generate dark current. A transfer gate empties the well into a floating diffusion shared by 8 cells, and a source follower drives the column. The read uses correlated double sampling: reset the floating diffusion and sample it, transfer the charge, sample again. The difference counts electrons and cancels both kTC noise and source-follower threshold mismatch, which is exactly what limits multi-level gain cells (A3 puts the margin at 62 mV for 3 bits). Writes meter a charge packet back through the transfer gate (fill-and-spill, as in CCDs), so levels are set by potential rather than by a leaky capacitor's history.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 capacitor wall (charge sits in a junction well, ~20 electrons per level); A1 #3 refresh (pinned wells leak ~0.1 electron/s at room temperature); A3 white space 1 (threshold variation in multi-level cells), handled by CDS.
ideas.step_change_claim: 4 bits/cell at roughly 1-beta area per bit (0.99-1.23x) with no capacitor. At or below 45 C, the 6-sigma-tail refresh interval is ~0.1-1 s and the median ~14-100 s, against 64 ms today. At 85 C, retention drops to DRAM-like levels (~3 ms tail for a 10-electron budget). So the win is multi-level sensing, plus refresh relief only for memory that runs cool.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: A conversion gain of 423 uV/electron implies a 379 aF floating diffusion; a 20-electron level spacing is 8.5 mV. Dark current is 0.1 electron/s at room temperature, assumed to double every ~7 C, with the 6-sigma tail at 100x the median. Retention for a 10-electron budget (median / tail): 100 s / 1 s at 25 C, 14 s / 0.14 s at 45 C, 1.9 s / 19 ms at 65 C, 0.26 s / 2.6 ms at 85 C. At DRAM bandwidth (50-500x the image-sensor readout bandwidth), noise is 1.6-4.9 electrons rms, which is 4-13 sigma per 20-electron level. Full well: 16 levels x 20 electrons = 320 electrons. A planar pinned well (~6,000 electrons/um2) would need 0.053 um2, 50x a 1-beta cell, so the well must be vertical: a 40 nm x 600 nm well has 0.075 um2 of sidewall and holds ~450 electrons. A 4,000-5,000 nm2 cell plus 1/8 of a 2,000 nm2 readout at 4 bits/cell gives 1,060-1,310 nm2/bit, 0.99-1.23x 1-beta. Read energy is ~4.5 fJ per 4-bit read on a 30 fF column. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-04)

ideas.name: Crystalline crested-barrier selector: transistor-less 1S1C crosspoint DRAM in stacked decks
ideas.one_liner: Replace the access transistor with a two-terminal crystalline 'crested' tunnel barrier whose current rises by many orders of magnitude between half-select and write voltage, and stack 2-4 crosspoint decks of short-bitline stub capacitors.
ideas.mechanism: Each cell is a stub capacitor (~14 nm x 300 nm, k ~40, ~0.9 fF) in series with a layered tunnel barrier at a 4F2 crosspoint. Likharev's crested profile (a thin high-barrier centre with lower flanks), or VARIOT's low-k/high-k/low-k stack, makes current extremely field-sensitive. At hold and half-select (V/2 or less) the barrier is effectively thick and leakage is limited by direct tunnelling. At write voltage the bands bend below the crest and Fowler-Nordheim current flows. The barrier must be crystalline (hBN/graphene stacks, AlN/GaN epitaxy or epitaxial oxides), not amorphous ALD, because the full write charge passes through it on every cycle. Bitlines are 64 cells long with sense amps under the array, and decks stack like 3D XPoint.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #4 litho (4F2 with no transistor; decks add bits); A1 #1 capacitor wall (short bitlines let a 300 nm stub suffice); A1 #7 periphery (moved under the array); A1 #2 3D (decks); A1 #3 (no transistor GIDL tail).
ideas.step_change_claim: Two decks at F = 20 nm give 1.34x 1-beta cell density; four decks give 2.7x, or 1.6x at F = 26 nm, which is reachable with SAQP and no EUV. No access-transistor GIDL tail.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Stub Cs = eps0*k*pi*d*h/t = 0.93 fF (k 40, 5 nm, 14 nm diameter, 300 nm tall). On a 64-cell bitline, Cbl = 7.8 fF and the signal is 56 mV (50 mV needed). The decisive number is charge fluence: each write passes 0.93 fC through a (20 nm)^2 selector, which is 2.3e-4 C/cm2. Amorphous barriers break down at Q_BD ~1-100 C/cm2, which allows only 4e3-4e5 writes: dead for DRAM-class use. 1e15 writes need Q_BD of at least 2.3e11 C/cm2. Crystalline resonant-tunnel-diode-class barriers carrying ~1e5 A/cm2 for 10 years (~3e13 C/cm2) [UNVERIFIED-PK] would allow ~1e17. Density: 1 / 2 / 4 decks of 4F2 at F = 20 nm give 0.67 / 1.34 / 2.67x 1-beta. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-05)

ideas.name: Seconds-ULTRARAM: a resonant-tunnelling floating gate retuned from 1,000-year retention to DRAM-class speed
ideas.one_liner: ULTRARAM's triple-barrier resonant-tunnelling gate blocks at 0 V, turns transparent at its resonance bias, and uses crystalline barriers. Trade its 1,000-year retention for ~1 s to 1 day and aim for 10 ns writes and 1e15 cycles.
ideas.mechanism: A floating gate above a III-V (or 2D) channel is isolated by a triple-barrier resonant-tunnelling stack. Two quantum wells of different thickness sit between three barriers and line up only at the programming bias (~2.5 V today), so electrons pass resonantly with no hot-carrier damage; off resonance the stack blocks. The read is a non-destructive channel-conductance measurement, making this a gain cell with no capacitor. The DRAM retune thins the barriers and wells, which lowers the retention target from 1,000 years to seconds or days, pulls the resonance voltage toward ~1-1.5 V and raises current density for ns writes. A 2D van der Waals version (graphene/hBN/MoS2 resonant barriers) could be transferred onto Si BEOL.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 (no capacitor: gain cell); A1 #3 refresh (retention tunable from 1 s to days); A1 #8 destructive read (read is non-destructive); A1 #10 voltage floor (resonant write at ~1-2.5 V).
ideas.step_change_claim: Refresh energy falls 1e3-1e6x (1 s to 1 day retention); writes cost ~1e-17-1e-16 J, against fJ-class DRAM cells plus periphery; crystalline barriers make 1e15-cycle endurance plausible.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Write current density for a floating-gate swing dV in time t is J = Cox*dV/t: 172 A/cm2 for 0.5 V in 10 ns (1,725 A/cm2 in 1 ns) at EOT ~1 nm. That is well inside resonant-tunnel-diode current densities (1e4-1e5 A/cm2 [UNVERIFIED-PK]), so the ~10 ms pulses measured on large single cells reflect the demo, not the physics. C*V^2 of a 20 nm cell at 2.5 V is 8.6e-17 J (Lancaster predicts ~1e-17 J). Relaxing retention from 1,000 years to 1 day removes ln(3.65e5) = 12.8 kT (0.33 eV) of barrier. By the charge-fluence rule (B5-05), only crystalline barriers survive 1e15 writes, and ULTRARAM's are epitaxial. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-06)

ideas.name: Self-timed NEMS-selector crosspoint: a two-terminal hysteretic nanorelay that charges the capacitor and lets go by itself
ideas.one_liner: Put a two-terminal nanorelay in series with each crosspoint capacitor. It snaps shut above its pull-in voltage, charges the capacitor until the voltage across it falls below release, then springs open: the write is self-limited, and during hold a vacuum gap means zero leakage.
ideas.mechanism: Each cell is a stub capacitor (~1 fF) plus a vertical or lateral 2D/ALD nanobeam relay (gap ~5 nm, stiffness ~1 N/m) at a 4F2 crosspoint. Relays have abrupt pull-in and release thresholds (effectively 0 mV/decade), so a half-select voltage below pull-in cannot close them. Write '1': the bitline at 2.2 V closes the relay; the capacitor charges until V_BL - V_cap drops below release (0.75 V); the relay opens and V_cap settles at ~1.45 V, set by mechanics rather than timing. Write '0': a slightly negative bitline leaves 0.45 V. Read: a bitline voltage between the two windows closes the relay only for '0' cells, producing a charge pulse (destructive, then restored). Hold: the gap is open vacuum, so leakage is through the capacitor dielectric only. Lines idle at mid-level and use V/3 biasing so unselected relays never see pull-in.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 leakage tail (no GIDL path through an open gap); A1 #4 litho (4F2 without a transistor, stackable decks); A1 #10 voltage floor (steep relay threshold); A1 #9 row hammer (a toggling line cannot inject charge through an open gap).
ideas.step_change_claim: Retention of 6-58 s at 1 fF (against 64 ms); 2-4 decks of 4F2 give 1.3-2.7x 1-beta density at F = 20 nm; the stored level is set by mechanics.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: V_pi = sqrt(8*k*g^3/(27*eps0*A)) = 1.45 V for k 1 N/m, g 5 nm, A 2e-15 m2. Release V_r = sqrt(2*k*g*gc^2/(eps0*A)) = 0.75 V with a 1 nm coated contact gap and no adhesion, a 0.69 V window. Self-limited write: V_cap = 2.2 - 0.75 = 1.45 V; '0' = 0.45 V. A 5% / 10% gap spread gives an 8% / 15% V_pi spread. Hold leakage of 8.6-86 aA through the capacitor dielectric (B1-18 numbers) gives 58-6 s for a 0.5 V budget on 1 fF. Mechanical f0 ~2.9 GHz, so closure takes ~0.1-0.3 ns. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-07)

ideas.name: Adiabatic refresh: recycle bitline and wordline charge with stepwise tanks or piezo-MEMS resonators
ideas.one_liner: Refresh is perfectly predictable and tolerant of latency, so charge bitlines and wordlines slowly through stepwise or resonant supplies and recover most of the energy. This is the acoustic revival: the piezoelectric resonator serves as an energy-recovery inductor rather than a delay line.
ideas.mechanism: During refresh (and optionally background activates), the VARY and VPP rails feeding a bank are ramped rather than fixed. The ramp comes from either (a) N-step tank-capacitor banks (stepwise charging) or (b) a resonant LC whose inductor is a compact AlN piezoelectric MEMS resonator or a package inductor, as in adiabatic or reversible logic. The sense amplifier makes its regenerative decision with a small non-adiabatic kick, then the bitline swing to VARY or 0 follows the ramped rails, and precharge returns charge to the tanks instead of shorting it. Wordlines (3 V, pumped at ~45% efficiency) are ramped the same way. No cell change is needed.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 refresh energy (16-33% of idle power); A1 #10 voltage floor (CV^2 energy is stuck); A2 white space 2 (use-phase energy is ~16x fab energy).
ideas.step_change_claim: Refresh energy per bit falls 2.4-3.2x (refresh-only 29.8 fJ to ~9-13 fJ), from ~12 mW to ~4 mW per 16Gb die, with no new cell and no new materials.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: A1 refresh is 2 x (BL 20.1 + WL 2.8 fJ) = 45.9 fJ. Refresh-only with a 1.3x periphery multiplier (no column or I/O path) is 29.8 fJ. Recovering the BL/WL CV^2 part gives: N=4 stepwise, 12.6 fJ (2.4x); N=8, 9.8 fJ (3.1x); resonant at 50% recovery (Vaire's first chip), 18.4 fJ (1.6x); resonant at 90%, 9.2 fJ (3.2x). One bank row is 8,192 bitlines x 34.7 fF = 284 pF, so resonance at 50 / 200 MHz needs 35.6 / 2.2 nH. On-chip spirals reach Q ~10; piezo-MEMS resonators reach Q ~1e3 [UNVERIFIED-PK]. The 16Gb die's refresh power goes from 12.2 mW to ~4 mW. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-08)

ideas.name: Negative-capacitance bitline: electrophysiology's capacitance neutralisation applied to the DRAM sense path
ideas.one_liner: Neuroscientists cancel the capacitance of long electrodes with a positive-feedback amplifier. Do the same on each DRAM bitline during charge sharing, and a 1.1 fF, ~260 nm stub capacitor gives today's 50 mV signal on an unchanged 512-cell bitline.
ideas.mechanism: A small amplifier per bitline (or a pre-phase folded into the existing sense amplifier) senses the bitline and drives a feedback capacitor Cf with gain A > 1. That injects a current equal to -Cn*dV/dt, with Cn = (A-1)*Cf. For the 1-2 ns of charge sharing, the bitline's effective capacitance becomes Cbl - Cn; then the neutraliser switches off and the normal latch fires. At Cn/Cbl ~0.7 the cell can shrink 3.3x for the same signal. Amplifier offset is auto-zeroed during precharge.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 storage-capacitor wall (the capacitor exists only to beat Cbl); A1 #10 voltage floor (more signal allows a lower VARY); A1 #2 3D (a short capacitor fits in a tier).
ideas.step_change_claim: Capacitor height falls from 1.3 um to ~260 nm (Cs 5.4 to 1.1 fF) at Cn/Cbl = 0.7, with the same 512-cell bitline. Cost: ~5-8% more periphery area (one amplifier per bitline) and no change to the array architecture.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: dV = Q/(Cs + Cbl - Cn), with Cbl = 34.7 fF. At Cn/Cbl = 0 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8: Cbl_eff is 34.7 / 17.4 / 10.4 / 6.9 fF; a 5.4 fF cell gives 71 / 125 / 179 / 230 mV; the Cs needed for 50 mV is 3.65 / 1.83 / 1.10 / 0.73 fF (pillar ~880 / 440 / 264 / 176 nm); amplifier-noise gain 1/(1 - Cn/Cbl) is 1 / 2 / 3.3 / 5. Offset: 10 mV on a 24 fF Cf injects 0.24 fC, against the 0.89 fC signal of a 1.7 fF cell; 3 mV injects 0.07 fC, which is acceptable with auto-zero. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-09)

ideas.name: Myelinated bitline: vacuum-sheathed bitline segments with non-latching 2T 'nodes of Ranvier'
ideas.one_liner: Nerves cut axon capacitance with an insulating sheath and regenerate the signal at nodes. Give DRAM bitlines a sealed vacuum sheath plus a 2-transistor oxide gain node every 32-64 cells, and the capacitor can be a ~150-300 nm stub.
ideas.mechanism: Bitlines are enclosed laterally in a sealed vacuum or air cavity, extending today's air spacers to the full bitline sidewall and the bitline-to-landing-pad gap. Every 32-64 cells the bitline breaks at a 'node': a BEOL IGZO 2T amplifier (source follower plus reset, non-latching) stacked above the array. The node turns the local segment's charge-sharing voltage into a current on a global bitline, and the main sense amp sits at the end as it does today. Unlike a local sense amplifier, the node neither latches nor restores, so it fits in BEOL above the array; restore runs through the global path.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 capacitor wall; A1 #10 voltage floor; A1 #2 3D (a short capacitor per tier); A1 #8 overfetch (segments allow sub-page activation).
ideas.step_change_claim: The Cs requirement falls from 3.65 to 0.6-0.8 fF (32-64-cell segments), so the capacitor is ~150-200 nm tall instead of ~1.3 um. The vacuum sheath alone lowers Cbl by only 1.5-1.7x.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Cbl split [ESTIMATE]: lateral bitline-to-bitline and bitline-to-contact 55%, bitline-to-wordline 25%, fixed 20%. A full vacuum sheath, starting from today's effective lateral k of 2.5-4, scales Cbl by x0.59-0.67. Segmenting to 512 / 128 / 64 / 32 cells gives Cbl of 34.7 / 11.7 / 7.8 / 5.9 fF, so Cs for 50 mV is 3.65 / 1.23 / 0.83 / 0.62 fF (~880 / 296 / 199 / 150 nm tall). Segmentation does most of the work; the sheath buys ~1.5x. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-10)

ideas.name: DNA-brick nanotrench templates for an EUV-free cell lattice
ideas.one_liner: DNA-brick crystals already align carbon nanotubes at 10.4 nm pitch with >95% yield. Use self-assembled DNA trenches, converted to inorganic hard masks, to pattern DRAM's perfectly periodic hole and line lattices instead of EUV or SAQP.
ideas.mechanism: On a wafer with coarse lithographic landing pads (ArF, ~80-100 nm), DNA-brick crystals assemble into nanotrench arrays whose pitch is programmable (10-40 nm) and whose registry is set by the pads. The DNA is mineralised (silicification or metal infiltration, as in sequential infiltration synthesis) or used directly as an etch mask, and the pattern transfers into a hardmask for the capacitor or channel holes, or for the bitline and wordline lines. Only the array layers use DNA; the periphery uses conventional lithography or sits on a bonded wafer. Because DNA is molecularly addressable, a single template can also carry non-periodic features such as pads and cuts.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #4 litho-bound scaling and EUV capital; A2 white space 3 (EUV-free, PFAS-light patterning).
ideas.step_change_claim: Replace up to 5-7 EUV exposures ($825-1,155 per wafer at 1c, per A1) with ~$0.5-25 of DNA per wafer and room-temperature aqueous assembly; pitch headroom is 3.4x finer than today's 35 nm capacitor pitch.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: A 10.4 nm pitch is 3.4x finer than the ~35 nm 1-beta capacitor pitch. Defects: 1.7e10 features per die at 95% assembly yield means 8.5e8 defects per die. Repair plus on-die ECC tolerates ~1e-4-1e-6 defects per feature, so a 500-50,000x improvement is needed; this is the core gap. A 20 nm DNA layer on a 300 mm wafer is 2.4 mg, or $0.48 per wafer at ~$200/g bioreactor scaffold pricing [UNVERIFIED-PK], or $24 per wafer at $10k/g. Lithography cost at risk: 5-7 EUV layers x ~$165 = $825-1,155 per wafer. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-11)

ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Error-correcting assembly (anneal protocols, proofreading tiles) plus defect-tolerant arrays (B2-15), using DNA only on repairable layers. (2) Use DNA only on cell layers above the transistors (the capacitor or hole lattice), or on a separate cell wafer bonded later (A3 white space 3); mineralise fully before any thermal step and minimise salt. (3) Graphoepitaxy in coarse lithographic trenches to confine domains; measure overlay statistically by SEM.
ideas.million_dollar_demo: With a DNA-nanotechnology lab, assemble DNA-brick trench crystals on 100 mm Si with ArF landing pads; convert them to SiO2/Al2O3 masks; etch 20-40 nm-pitch holes 500 nm deep; measure defect density over cm2 by e-beam inspection (~$300k including DNA synthesis and inspection time). Success means 1e-4 defects per feature over 1 cm2 and a working 1 kb capacitor array patterned this way.
ideas.resource_angle: Cuts dependence on EUV (ASML is the only supplier; each tool draws ~10 GWh/yr) and on resists (~90% Japanese). Assembly is aqueous and at room temperature, and DNA is biomanufactured from sugars.
ideas.us_buildable: Harvard Wyss Institute/Yin lab, ASU Biodesign Institute, Caltech, Brookhaven CFN (DNA-assembled materials); etch at Harvard CNS or Brookhaven CFN.

ideas.name: Voltage-clocked skyrmion shift register: magnetic bubble memory revived with gate clocks instead of currents
ideas.one_liner: Move ~20 nm skyrmions along a magnetic track with a two-phase ladder of voltage gates (VCMA), CCD-style, so no current flows along the track; read at the end with a skyrmionic MTJ.
ideas.mechanism: A chiral multilayer (Pt/Co/MgO type, with perpendicular anisotropy and strong DMI) is patterned into tracks 2F wide. Gates at 2F pitch on 1.5 nm MgO modulate interface anisotropy through VCMA. Two-phase clocks with a built-in ratchet (an asymmetric gate profile) create a moving energy minimum that carries each skyrmion one bit-length per clock, like charge packets in a CCD. A skyrmionic MTJ at the track end reads the bit (20-70% contrast reported), and a VCMA/SOT nucleator writes it. The state is non-volatile between shifts. With no lateral current there is no electromigration or Joule heating, and thousands of tracks share each clock line.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 refresh (non-volatile); A1 #1 capacitor (none); A1 #9 row hammer (no charge); A2 use-phase energy.
ideas.step_change_claim: [SPECULATIVE] Refresh goes to zero; ~47 aJ per gate toggle; no capacitor or access transistor per bit. Density is 1.34x WORSE than 1-beta per layer at F = 13.4 nm (parity needs F ~11.6 nm or two layers). This is an energy and volatility play, not density.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: VCMA drive: xi = 100 fJ/(V.m) x 1 V/1.5 nm gives dK_s = 6.7e-5 J/m2; over pi*(10 nm)^2 that is 2.1e-20 J = 5 kT per skyrmion step, far below typical pinning (tens of kT), so it is too weak. xi = 1,000 fJ/(V.m) would give 51 kT. Area: a 2F track x 4F bit = 8F2, which is 1,436 nm2 at F = 13.4 nm (1.34x 1-beta area) and 3,200 nm2 at F = 20 nm. Gate C = 47 aF, so 47 aJ per toggle. A 64-bit track averaging 32 steps at ~1 ns gives 32 ns latency and ~190 fJ per random access. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-12)

ideas.novelty: TWIST on known. Magnetic bubble memory (Bell Labs and Intel, 1970s) used a global rotating field, and skyrmion racetracks (Fert, Parkin and others) use currents. Voltage-gated anisotropy ratchets for skyrmions have been proposed [UNVERIFIED-PK]. Combining a CCD-style two-phase VCMA clock with the 2024 all-electrical skyrmion MTJ readout is the twist.
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) VCMA is too weak: 5 kT per step at xi = 100, against pinning disorder in sputtered films. (2) Room-temperature stability of skyrmions of 20 nm or less (needs at least ~45 kT), and skyrmion Hall deflection at track edges. (3) Serial access latency of tens of ns, and density no better than DRAM per layer.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Stronger gating: magneto-ionic (H+ or O2- gating) or ferroelectric-gated anisotropy gives ~10x larger dK, or add small SOT assist pulses. (2) Synthetic-antiferromagnet or ferrimagnetic skyrmions, which have no Hall angle and are smaller and more stable. (3) Short 16-32-bit tracks in parallel, as a non-volatile buffer tier.
ideas.million_dollar_demo: Grow chiral multilayers at a university magnetics lab, pattern 5-gate tracks, image skyrmion motion under gate clocks by MOKE and X-ray microscopy at a national lab, and integrate an end-of-track MTJ (~$400k). Success means deterministic multi-step transport of single skyrmions at 1.5 V or less, at least 1e9 clock cycles, and an error rate below 1e-6 per step.
ideas.resource_angle: Uses nm-thin films of Pt and Ir (Pt is concentrated in South Africa [UNVERIFIED-PK]), so the mass is small. No Hf, Ru or high-aspect-ratio etch.
ideas.us_buildable: University magnetics labs (University of Minnesota, MIT, Johns Hopkins, Cornell); X-ray microscopy at Berkeley Lab ALS or Argonne APS; NIST CNST.

ideas.name: Altermagnetic tunnel-junction RAM: MRAM without stray fields
ideas.one_liner: Altermagnets have spin-split bands like ferromagnets but zero net magnetisation like antiferromagnets. Junctions built from them could read out by TMR with no dipolar crosstalk and with THz-scale dynamics, packing non-volatile bits ~1.5 diameters apart.
ideas.mechanism: The free layer is an altermagnet (RuO2, CrSb, MnTe or newer candidates) whose Neel vector sets spin-dependent tunnelling through an MgO-type barrier to a reference electrode. Writing uses spin-splitter or spin-orbit torque from an adjacent line, or the altermagnet's own current-induced torque; reading uses TMR. Zero net moment removes dipolar coupling to neighbours and to external fields, so crosspoint pitch can drop from ~2.5 to ~1.5 diameters, and exchange-enhanced switching could reach ps timescales. Endurance is magnetic, with no wear mechanism.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 refresh (non-volatile); A1 #1 capacitor (none); A1 #9 row hammer; A1 #4 density through tighter pitch.
ideas.step_change_claim: [SPECULATIVE] 2.8x denser than ferromagnetic MTJ crosspoints at the same diameter (900 vs 2,500 nm2 at d = 20 nm), ~1.2x 1-beta per deck; non-volatile; potential ps writes.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: A ferromagnetic MTJ crosspoint needs pitch ~2.5 d (50 nm at d = 20 nm), 2,500 nm2/bit. An altermagnet at ~1.5 d (30 nm) needs 900 nm2/bit: 2.8x denser, 1.19x 1-beta per deck, 2.4x with two decks. The read needs roughly 100% TMR or more for ns sensing. Measured altermagnetic TMR is small, and whether RuO2 is altermagnetic at all is debated; theory predicts more than 1,000% for CrSb/In2Se3/Fe3GaTe2 stacks. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-13)

evidence.shows: First experimental evidence that TMR depends on spin direction in altermagnetic junctions; magnitude still to be increased; RuO2's altermagnetism remains debated (via search snippet).

ideas.novelty: [SPECULATIVE] new physics. Altermagnetism was established in 2022-24 [UNVERIFIED-PK], and the first junction TMR in RuO2 was reported in 2025 (UNIST). A memory-cell design is early-stage, and no array exists.
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) TMR magnitude is tiny so far, and RuO2 may not be altermagnetic. (2) Deterministic switching of the Neel vector at or below 1e11 A/m2 is unproven. (3) Materials: films are epitaxial; Ru is A2-flagged (fleet use as electrodes would need 26-176% of world Ru); CrSb (Sb) and MnTe (Te) carry supply-concentration risk.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Screen CrSb, MnTe and KV2Se2O-type candidates, including with ferroelectric barriers, for large TMR. (2) Borrow antiferromagnetic SOT switching results (CuMnAs, Mn3Sn) [UNVERIFIED-PK]. (3) Choose Ru-free altermagnets.
ideas.million_dollar_demo: Grow altermagnet films by MBE or sputtering at an oxide-MBE facility; fabricate 50-200 nm junctions; measure TMR against temperature and SOT switching (~$400k). Success means at least 50% TMR at 300 K and deterministic switching at 5e11 A/m2 or less.

ideas.us_buildable: Cornell PARADIM (oxide MBE), Penn State 2DCC, NIST CNST, university spintronics groups.

ideas.name: 77 K oxide MLC gain-cell stage for cryogenic and superconducting computers
ideas.one_liner: imec's superconducting-digital blade already puts 'cryo-DRAM' on a 77 K interposer. Build that memory from oxide gain cells, which at 77 K hold data for hours, store 3-4 bits per cell and run the array at 0.4 V.
ideas.mechanism: IGZO/IWO 2T0C gain cells (no capacitor) sit in BEOL tiers on a 77 K cryo-CMOS periphery wafer. At 77 K, oxide-cell leakage collapses (8,000 s reported for IGZO 2T0C) and threshold drift (PBTI, hydrogen motion) is thermally frozen. Si subthreshold swing falls to ~15-20 mV/decade, so periphery and wordlines run at ~0.4 / 1.0 V, and Cu resistance drops several-fold. Together these make 3-4 bits/cell with write-verify realistic. The stage links to 4 K superconducting logic through the thermal-break link in imec's architecture.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 refresh (1e5x fewer); A1 #10 voltage floor (0.4 V array); A1 #5 data movement (memory next to cold compute rather than at 300 K); A3's cryo revival condition ('where the cooling is already paid for').
ideas.step_change_claim: Array energy x0.13 (0.78 vs 5.9 pJ per useful bit); refresh cut ~1e5x; 3-4 bits/cell gives 1.2-1.6x 1-beta density per tier, ~17,000x the density of the best 4 K superconducting memory array.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Energy scale (VARY 1.05 -> 0.4 V, WL 2.9 -> 1.0 V): x0.13, giving 0.78 pJ per useful bit cold. With A3's 77 K penalty of 9.7-19.3 W/W, that is 7.6-15 pJ at the wall against 5.9 pJ for a warm core: it loses for warm compute and wins only when the compute is already cold. Retention of 8,000 s instead of 64 ms means 1.25e5x fewer refreshes. A gain cell at 2.5x the 1T1C area storing 2 / 3 / 4 bits gives 0.8 / 1.2 / 1.6x 1-beta per tier. The best superconducting array is 2.6e-5 Gb/mm2, so a 1-beta-class array is 17,192x denser. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-14)

ideas.novelty: TWIST on known. Cold DRAM at 77 K (Rambus and Microsoft, 2017) and imec's 77 K cryo-DRAM tier are KNOWN, and IGZO 2T0C has been measured at 77 K (A3). The new part is an oxide multi-level gain-cell stage designed for the 77 K tier: frozen drift enables MLC, with no refresh and a 0.4 V array.
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) It is only worth building if superconducting or cryogenic compute happens; A3 killed cold memory for warm data centres. (2) Oxide mobility drops at 77 K (percolation and hopping in a-IGZO), cutting read current and speed. (3) Bandwidth and heat leak of the 4 K-77 K link.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Revival condition: a superconducting or 77 K cryo-CMOS AI system ships (imec SCD), at which point this becomes the default memory. (2) Crystalline or In-rich oxides (IWO, In2O3) with band transport keep mobility at 77 K. (3) Superconducting flex links.
ideas.million_dollar_demo: Fabricate IGZO/IWO 2T0C arrays on a university BEOL line; characterise 3-4-bit write-verify, retention and speed at 77 K in a cryoprober; tape out a cryo-CMOS sense/ADC chip on a 22 nm or 130 nm MPW and test it in LN2 (~$350k). Success means 3 bits/cell, at least 1 h retention and reads of 20 ns or less at 77 K.
ideas.resource_angle: Cold operation cuts array energy ~7x, and oxide cells avoid capacitor Hf and Ru. IGZO carries the Ga flag; IWO or ITZO avoids it.
ideas.us_buildable: Purdue Birck, Georgia Tech IEN or Notre Dame (oxide BEOL); cryogenic probing at NIST Boulder; cryo-CMOS MPW at GlobalFoundries (Malta, NY).

ideas.name: Superconducting kinetic-inductance memory with frequency-multiplexed readout (4 K)
ideas.one_liner: Store a flux quantum as loss-free persistent current in a nanowire loop. Kinetic inductance lets loops shrink toward ~0.1 um2, and astronomy's frequency-multiplexed resonator readout cuts the wires that leak heat into 4 K.
ideas.mechanism: Each cell is a NbN (or similar) nanowire loop whose kinetic inductance (~70 pH per square) holds a persistent current; one flux quantum is one bit. Heater cryotrons (hTrons) or nanocryotrons drive a branch normal to write and to read. Row-column arrays exist (MIT and NIST). The twist: each column's sense element is a superconducting resonator at its own frequency on a shared feedline (MKID-style), so thousands of columns read out through one coax and 4 K wiring heat drops sharply.
ideas.which_bottleneck: The cryogenic memory gap for superconducting compute (A3 section 2.11); A1 #5 data movement at 4 K; energy per bit.
ideas.step_change_claim: Intrinsic energy per operation is ~1e-20-1e-17 J (I*Phi0 ~2-6e-20 J), against ~fJ for CMOS. Density, however, is only 2.6e-5 Gb/mm2 today (1/17,000 of DDR5) and ~0.005 Gb/mm2 at best (1/90): an L1/L2-class memory for SFQ logic, not a DRAM replacement.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: The reported 2.6 Mb/cm2 is 2.6e-5 Gb/mm2. L_k = hbar*R_sq/(pi*Delta) = 69 pH/square (R_sq 500 ohm, Tc 10 K). One flux quantum at 10 uA needs 207 pH, i.e. 3 squares (150 nm of 50 nm wire); at 30 uA, 1 square. Stored energy I*Phi0 is 2.1-6.2e-20 J. Scaled cells of 0.5 / 0.1 um2 (loop plus two hTrons, 0.5 efficiency) give 0.001 / 0.005 Gb/mm2, 1/447 to 1/89 of DDR5. At a 4 K penalty of 300-1,000 W/W, 1e-17 J cold costs 3-10 fJ at the wall. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-15)

evidence.shows: Loss-free persistent-current loop; whole cell 3 x 7 um; ~10 fJ dissipation; BER below 1e-7; kinetic inductance allows scaling compared with Josephson-junction memories (via search snippet).

(2) Heater-raised cell inductance (reported) and ns thermal time constants limit speed. (3) The cost of 4 K cooling, and very limited fab capacity.

ideas.name: 1T-TaS2 charge-configuration memory: picosecond, attojoule switching for the 4 K tier
ideas.one_liner: A single ~2 ps electrical pulse flips thin 1T-TaS2 between insulating and metastable metallic charge-ordered states at ~9.4 fJ/um2, ~24 aJ for a 50 nm device: a natural memory for superconducting logic.
ideas.mechanism: Thin 1T-TaS2 flakes or films sit between two electrodes. A ps current pulse reorders the charge-density-wave domain configuration into a metastable 'hidden' metallic state (low resistance), and a longer, weaker pulse restores the insulating Mott-CDW state. The state is non-volatile at cryogenic temperature and is read resistively. Cells form a 4F2 crosspoint with selectors, or 1T1R with cryo-CMOS.
ideas.which_bottleneck: The cryogenic memory gap; energy per bit; write speed matched to SFQ logic (ps).
ideas.step_change_claim: Write energy of ~24-94 aJ at 50-100 nm and ~2 ps (0.5 ps floor), ~100x below the superconducting nanowire memory's ~10 fJ cell energy; 0.67x 1-beta density per deck at F = 20 nm if the crosspoint works.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: 9.4 fJ/um2 x (0.05 um)^2 = 24 aJ; x (0.1 um)^2 = 94 aJ. The intrinsic switching floor is ~0.5 ps. A 4F2 crosspoint at F = 20 / 40 nm gives 0.67 / 0.17x 1-beta per deck. At ~500 W/W of 4 K cooling, 24 aJ costs ~12 fJ at the wall. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-16)

ideas.name: Quantum-dot charge RAM at 4 K: spin-qubit process lines repurposed for dense cryogenic memory
ideas.one_liner: Gate-defined silicon quantum dots are the densest controllable charge boxes ever built. At 4 K a pinched-off barrier holds ~20 electrons essentially forever, so a 70-100 nm dot cell gives 0.05-0.1 Gb/mm2, 2,000-4,000x the best superconducting memory.
ideas.mechanism: On a 300 mm Si/SiGe or Si-MOS spin-qubit process, each cell is a gate-defined dot (plunger gate) with a barrier gate to a shared reservoir lead. A bit is 'full' (~10-30 electrons) or 'empty'; Coulomb blockade is not needed, only the barrier. Write: open the barrier (ns tunnelling) with the plunger set. Hold: the barrier is pinched off, so tunnel rates are far below 1e-6/s and thermal activation over ~50 meV (~140 kT) is impossible at 4 K. Read: a single-electron-transistor charge sensor shared by 4-8 dots, or gate reflectometry, with crossbar-shared gate lines. Cryo-CMOS drives the lines.
ideas.which_bottleneck: The cryogenic memory capacity gap (superconducting arrays reach 2.6 Mb/cm2); data movement at 4 K; memory for superconducting and quantum control.
ideas.step_change_claim: 0.05-0.1 Gb/mm2 (0.11-0.23x DDR5) at 4 K, ~2,000-4,000x denser than superconducting memory arrays; gate writes of 25-400 zJ (12-200 aJ at the wall); no refresh.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Cells of 100 / 70 nm at 0.5 efficiency give 0.050 / 0.102 Gb/mm2, which is 0.11 / 0.23x 1-beta and 1,923 / 3,925x the 2.6 Mb/cm2 superconducting array. A dot of r = 15 nm has C_sigma ~39 aF and E_c = 2.1 meV = 6 kT at 4.2 K (0.3 kT at 77 K, so 4 K only), but storing ~20 electrons against 0 needs no blockade. A 50 meV barrier is 138 kT at 4.2 K and only 7.5 kT at 77 K. Gate write: 10 aF x (0.05-0.2 V)^2 = 25-400 zJ; at ~500 W/W, 12-200 aJ at the wall. Read: an SET at 1 nA for 50 ns integrates 312 electrons, a shot-noise SNR of ~18. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-17)

evidence.title: Medeiros et al., scalable superconducting nanowire memory (arXiv 2503.22897)
evidence.shows: The best superconducting array density (2.6 Mb/cm2) defines the cryogenic memory gap this cell targets (via search snippet).

evidence.title: imec IMAPS 2025 SCD blade presentation

ideas.novelty: NEW combination. Single-electron memories at 4 K date to the 1990s [UNVERIFIED-PK], and dense gate-defined dot arrays are a quantum-computing process line. Using a 300 mm spin-qubit line as a classical cryogenic memory fab, with relaxed many-electron bits, did not appear in the literature searched.

(2) Read speed: qubit charge sensing takes us for 1e-3 errors; memory needs 50 ns or less at 1e-12. (3) Crossbar addressing of dense gates (fan-out), plus charge noise and drift.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Many-electron bits with wide voltage windows; per-row calibration tables held in the controller. (2) A dedicated SET per few dots with cryo-CMOS amplifiers on the 4 K stage. (3) Borrow crossbar-network addressing proposals from qubit work [UNVERIFIED-PK].

ideas.name: TSV-free inductive stacking for short memory-on-logic stacks
ideas.one_liner: Replace TSVs and microbumps with on-chip coils (ThruChip-style inductive coupling) in 2-4-high DRAM-on-logic stacks. That removes the TSV process and part of the HBM area tax, but the physics limits it to short stacks.
ideas.mechanism: Dies thinned to ~10 um are glued rather than bump-bonded. Data crosses between stacked dies through pairs of ~30 um on-chip spiral coils at ~8 Gb/s each. Power and ground use a few highly doped silicon vias or edge connections. There is no TSV etch or fill, no microbump yield loss and no hybrid-bond overlay.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM TSV/stacking tax (~3x wafer per bit); A1 #5 data movement (memory directly on logic).
ideas.step_change_claim: For 4-high stacks: no TSV or microbump process steps, ~26% less die area than TSVs (reported for a 7 nm SRAM stack), and ~2.7 pJ/b on the worst-case hop. For 16-high HBM it fails: 62-562 mm2 of coil per die, or 13.5 pJ/b through relays.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: HBM4-class bandwidth of 2,048 x 8 Gb/s = 16.4 Tb/s needs 1,928 links at 8.5 Gb/s. Coil diameter must roughly match the coupling distance. A 16-high stack of 30 um dies needs 450 um coils, i.e. 562 mm2 of coil per die (impossible); with 10 um dies, 62 mm2 (still impossible); a 4-high stack of 10 um dies needs 2 mm2 (fine). The relay alternative costs 0.9 pJ/b per hop, 13.5 pJ/b to the top of a 16-high stack against ~3-4 pJ/b for HBM in total. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-18)

ideas.novelty: KNOWN (Kuroda group at Keio, ThruChip Japan, University of Tokyo 2022). The card's contribution is the reach and area arithmetic: viable for 2-4-high memory-on-logic, not for 16-high HBM.
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) Coupling reach scales with coil diameter, so tall stacks need huge coils. (2) Power delivery still needs vias. (3) Bandwidth density (2.7 Gb/s/mm2 for 2015-era relays) is far below hybrid bonding.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Restrict to 4-high or less, and get height from monolithic tiers instead (B3/B4). (2) Highly doped silicon vias for power. (3) Raise per-link rates with resonant coupling.
ideas.million_dollar_demo: An MPW logic die plus a DRAM-like test die with coils, thinned to 10-20 um and glue-stacked 2-4 high at a packaging lab; measure BER, pJ/b and crosstalk (~$300k).
ideas.resource_angle: Removes TSV copper fill and microbump solder (Sn, Ag) and lowers stacking capital; adds no scarce elements.
ideas.us_buildable: Georgia Tech Packaging Research Center, NY CREATES (Albany), plus a U.S. MPW for the dies.
